Two separate pieces are joined by “**or**” ($x<A$ or $x>B$), never by “and”, because no number is in both."},{"k":"fig","id":"w09-min","caption":"A minimum graph: negative between the roots."}],"figs":["w09-min"]},{"title":"Quadratic inequalities","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Solving $ax^2+bx+c>0$ (or $<$, $\\ge$, $\\le$)","blocks":[{"k":"ol","items":["Rearrange so that one side is 0.","Find the **critical values**: the roots of $ax^2+bx+c=0$.","Decide the sign in each interval, by the shape of the graph or by a **sign diagram**.","Write the answer as an interval or a pair of intervals."]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w09-signs","caption":"A sign diagram for $(x+2)(x-1)$."},{"k":"p","text":"From a graph, “$f(x)>k$” is read by drawing the line $y=k$: the answer is where the curve is **above** the line."}],"figs":["w09-signs"]},{"title":"Modelling with quadratics","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"life","title":"Typical models","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Projectiles:** $H=ut-\\tfrac12gt^2$ (or $H=h_0+ut-5t^2$ in metres). The maximum height is at the vertex; the object lands when $H=0$.","**Arches and bridges:** $H=kx(w-x)$ has roots $0$ and $w$ (the span) and its greatest height at $x=\\tfrac w2$.","**Areas with a fixed perimeter**, **profit** from price, and **revenue** from sales.","**Motion:** a car accelerating from rest covers $s=\\tfrac12at^2$; a vehicle at constant speed covers $s=vt+s_0$; they meet where the curve and line intersect."]}]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Context first","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A time before launch or after landing, a negative length, or a fraction of a person has no meaning. (b) Find the range of values of $x$ for which (i) $y$ decreases (ii) $y$ increases (iii) $y$ is positive (iv) $y$ is negative."}],"steps":["(a) $y$ for $x=-4$ to $3$: 10, 4, 0, −2, −2, 0, 4, 10.","Line of symmetry $x=-0.5$; minimum $y=0.25-0.5-2=-2.25$.","(b)(i) $y$ decreases for $x<-0.5$; (ii) increases for $x>-0.5$.","(iii) $y>0$ for $x<-2$ or $x>1$.","(iv) $y<0$ for $-2<x<1$."],"answer":"(i) $x<-0.5$ (ii) $x>-0.5$ (iii) $x<-2$ or $x>1$ (iv) $-2<x<1$","figs":[]},{"title":"Reading ranges from pre-drawn graphs","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Graph P is a U-shaped curve crossing the $x$-axis at $-20$ and $10$. For each, find (a) where $y\\le0$ and where $y>0$ (b) the line of symmetry (c) where $y$ increases."}],"steps":["(a) P: $y\\le0$ for $-20\\le x\\le10$; $y>0$ for $x<-20$ or $x>10$.","Q: $y\\le0$ for $x\\le-2$ or $x\\ge6$; $y>0$ for $-2<x<6$.","(b) P: $x=\\dfrac{-20+10}{2}=-5$. Q: $x=\\dfrac{-2+6}{2}=2$.","(c) P (minimum) increases for $x>-5$. Q (maximum) increases for $x<2$."],"answer":"P: $y\\le0$ on $-20\\le x\\le10$; symmetry $x=-5$. Q: $y>0$ on $-2<x<6$; symmetry $x=2$.","figs":["w09-read"]},{"title":"Quadratic inequalities by sign diagram","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Solve (a) $x^2-x-6<0$ (b) $2x^2+5x-3\\ge0$ (c) $x^2+x-2>0$."}],"steps":["(a) $(x-3)(x+2)<0$. Critical values $-2$, $3$. The product is negative between them: $-2<x<3$.","(b) $(2x-1)(x+3)\\ge0$. Critical values $-3$, $\\tfrac12$. Positive or zero outside: $x\\le-3$ or $x\\ge\\tfrac12$.","(c) $(x+2)(x-1)>0$. From the sign diagram (Figure 9.3): $x<-2$ or $x>1$."],"answer":"(a) $-2<x<3$ (b) $x\\le-3$ or $x\\ge\\tfrac12$ (c) $x<-2$ or $x>1$","figs":[]},{"title":"Above a given level","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"For $y=4+3x-x^2$, find the values of $x$ for which $y\\ge2$, (a) from the graph (b) by calculation."}],"steps":["(a) Draw $y=2$ on the graph of Example 9.1; it meets the curve at $x\\approx-0.6$ and $x\\approx3.6$. The curve is above the line between them.","(b) $4+3x-x^2\\ge2$ gives $x^2-3x-2\\le0$.","Roots: $x=\\dfrac{3\\pm\\sqrt{9+8}}{2}=\\dfrac{3\\pm\\sqrt{17}}{2}\\approx-0.56$ or $3.56$.","So $-0.56\\le x\\le3.56$."],"answer":"$-0.56\\le x\\le3.56$","figs":[]},{"title":"A ball thrown upwards","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A ball is launched vertically from the ground at 80 ft/s; its height is $H=80t-16t^2$ feet after $t$ seconds. (e) When does the ball hit the ground?"}],"steps":["(a) $H$: 0, 36, 64, 84, 96, 100, 96, 64, 36, 0.","(c)(i) $H=64$ at $t=1$ and $t=4$, so $H<64$ for $0\\le t<1$ or $4<t\\le5$.","(ii) $H=36$ at $t=0.5$ and $t=4.5$, so $H>36$ for $0.5<t<4.5$.","(iii) Increasing for $0\\le t<2.5$; (iv) decreasing for $2.5<t\\le5$.","(d) Maximum 100 ft at $t=2.5$ s.","(e) $H=0$: $16t(5-t)=0$, so $t=5$ s."],"answer":"(c)(i) $0\\le t<1$ or $4<t\\le5$ (ii) $0.5<t<4.5$ (d) 100 ft at 2.5 s (e) 5 s","figs":["w09-ball"]},{"title":"Intervals of height","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"An object’s height is $H=60t-12t^2$ feet. (c) Find the maximum height. (d) When does it land?"}],"steps":["(a) $H$: 0, 27, 48, 63, 72, 75, 72, 63, 48, 27, 0.","(b)(i) $60t-12t^2=63$ gives $4t^2-20t+21=0$, $(2t-3)(2t-7)=0$: $t=1.5$ or $3.5$. So $H<63$ for $0\\le t<1.5$ or $3.5<t\\le5$.","(ii) $60t-12t^2=48$ gives $t^2-5t+4=0$: $t=1$ or $4$. So $H>48$ for $1<t<4$.","(iii) increasing for $0\\le t<2.5$; (iv) decreasing for $2.5<t\\le5$.","(c) 75 ft at $t=2.5$ s. (d) $12t(5-t)=0$: $t=5$ s."],"answer":"(b)(i) $0\\le t<1.5$ or $3.5<t\\le5$ (ii) $1<t<4$ (c) 75 ft (d) 5 s","figs":["w09-assess"]},{"title":"A parabolic archway","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The entrance to an athletic field is a parabolic arch $H=12x-x^2$, where $H$ ft is the height of the arch at $x$ ft from one foot. (a) Tabulate $H$ for $x=0$ to $12$ and draw the graph. (b) Find the values of $x$ where the arch is 30 ft high. (c) Find where the arch is higher than 25 ft. (d) Find the maximum height and the span. (e) Can a 4 m (about 13 ft) wide lorry, 30 ft high, pass through the centre?"}],"steps":["(a) $H$ for $x=0,1,\\dots,12$: 0, 11, 20, 27, 32, 35, 36, 35, 32, 27, 20, 11, 0.","(b) $x^2-12x+30=0$: $x=6\\pm\\sqrt6\\approx3.55$ or $8.45$.","(c) $x^2-12x+25<0$: roots $6\\pm\\sqrt{11}\\approx2.68$ and $9.32$, so $2.68<x<9.32$.","(d) Maximum 36 ft at $x=6$; span 12 ft (the roots are 0 and 12).","(e) At height 30 ft the arch is only $8.45-3.55=4.9$ ft wide, much less than 13 ft. **No.**"],"answer":"(b) 3.55 and 8.45 (c) $2.68<x<9.32$ (d) 36 ft; 12 ft (e) no","figs":["w09-arch"]},{"title":"A car and a bus","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A car starts from rest at a junction and covers $s=t^2$ metres in $t$ seconds. At the same moment a bus 20 m ahead travels at a steady 8 m/s, so $s=8t+20$. (a) When and where does the car catch the bus? (b) For what times is the bus ahead? (c) How far apart are they after 4 s, and when is the bus furthest ahead?"}],"steps":["(a) $t^2=8t+20$ gives $t^2-8t-20=0$, $(t-10)(t+2)=0$: $t=10$ s (reject $-2$). Then $s=100$ m.","(b) The bus is ahead while $8t+20>t^2$, that is $0\\le t<10$.","(c) Gap $=8t+20-t^2$. At $t=4$: $32+20-16=36$ m.","The gap $-t^2+8t+20$ is greatest at $t=4$; so after 4 s the bus is furthest ahead, by 36 m."],"answer":"(a) after 10 s, 100 m from the junction (b) $0\\le t<10$ (c) 36 m, at 4 s","figs":["w09-chase"]},{"title":"A rectangle with fixed perimeter","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A rectangle has perimeter 36 cm and width $x$ cm. (a) Show that its area is $A=x(18-x)$. (b) For what widths is the area at least 72 cm²? (c) For what widths does the area increase as $x$ increases?"}],"steps":["(a) Length $=18-x$, so $A=x(18-x)$.","(b) $18x-x^2\\ge72$ gives $x^2-18x+72\\le0$, $(x-6)(x-12)\\le0$: $6\\le x\\le12$.","(c) Vertex at $x=9$: $A$ increases for $0<x<9$."],"answer":"(b) $6\\le x\\le12$ (c) $0<x<9$","figs":[]},{"title":"When is the business profitable?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A firm’s weekly profit from selling $x$ crates is $P=-x^2+70x-600$ (GH₵). (a) For what numbers of crates does the firm make a profit? (b) For what values of $x$ does the profit increase? (c) Find the maximum profit. (d) The owner wants a profit of at least GH₵400. Find the range of sales."}],"steps":["(a) $P>0$: $x^2-70x+600<0$, $(x-10)(x-60)<0$: $10<x<60$.","(b) Vertex at $x=35$: profit increases for $x<35$.","(c) $P(35)=-1225+2450-600=625$, that is GH₵625.","(d) $-x^2+70x-600\\ge400$ gives $x^2-70x+1000\\le0$, $(x-20)(x-50)\\le0$: $20\\le x\\le50$ crates."],"answer":"(a) $10<x<60$ (b) $x<35$ (c) GH₵625 (d) 20 to 50 crates","figs":[]},{"title":"A water fountain","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A jet of water from a fountain follows $h=2+3x-0.5x^2$, where $h$ m is the height at a horizontal distance $x$ m from the nozzle. (a) Find the greatest height. (b) For what distances is the water more than 4 m high? (c) Where does the water hit the ground?"}],"steps":["(a) Vertex at $x=-\\dfrac{3}{2(-0.5)}=3$: $h=2+9-4.5=6.5$ m.","(b) $2+3x-0.5x^2>4$ gives $x^2-6x+4<0$; roots $3\\pm\\sqrt5\\approx0.76$ and $5.24$. So $0.76<x<5.24$.","(c) $0.5x^2-3x-2=0$ gives $x^2-6x-4=0$, $x=3+\\sqrt{13}\\approx6.61$ m (reject the negative root)."],"answer":"(a) 6.5 m (b) $0.76<x<5.24$ (c) about 6.61 m","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results","items":["Increasing/decreasing changes at the line of symmetry $x=-\\dfrac{b}{2a}$.","For roots $A<B$: if $a>0$, $y<0$ for $A<x<B$ and $y>0$ for $x<A$ or $x>B$; reverse for $a<0$.","Solve inequalities: rearrange to 0, find critical values, use the graph or a sign diagram.","$f(x)>k$: where the curve is above the line $y=k$.","In models: vertex = greatest or least value; roots = start/landing or break-even; always state the domain."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"For $y=x^2-4x+1$, $y$ increases as $x$ increases when","options":["$x>2$","$x<2$","$x>-2$","$x<-2$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Minimum at $x=2$; it rises after the minimum."},{"q":"A ∩-shaped graph has roots $-3$ and $5$. $y$ is positive when","options":["$-3<x<5$","$x<-3$ or $x>5$","$x>5$","$x<-3$"],"correct":0,"explain":"It is above the axis between the roots."},{"q":"The solution of $x^2-9<0$ is","options":["$-3<x<3$","$x<-3$ or $x>3$","$x<3$","$x>-3$"],"correct":0,"explain":"$(x-3)(x+3)<0$ between the roots."},{"q":"The solution of $(x-1)(x-4)\\ge0$ is","options":["$x\\le1$ or $x\\ge4$","$1\\le x\\le4$","$x\\ge4$","$x\\le1$ and $x\\ge4$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Outside the roots; joined by “or”."},{"q":"$H=40t-5t^2$. The time when $H$ is greatest is","options":["4 s","8 s","2 s","5 s"],"correct":0,"explain":"$t=-\\dfrac{40}{-10}=4$."},{"q":"$H=40t-5t^2$. The object is higher than 60 m for","options":["$2<t<6$","$0<t<2$","$6<t<8$","$t>6$"],"correct":0,"explain":"$t^2-8t+12<0$, roots 2 and 6."},{"q":"An arch $H=x(10-x)$ has its greatest height at","options":["$x=5$, $H=25$","$x=10$, $H=0$","$x=5$, $H=50$","$x=2.5$, $H=18.75$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Halfway across the span."},{"q":"A car covers $s=2t^2$ and a cyclist $s=6t$. For how long is it above 25 m?","a":"$t^2-6t+5<0$: $1<t<5$, 4 s"},{"q":"An arch is $H=0.5x(16-x)$ m. Find its span, its height and the width at a height of 24 m.","a":"16 m; 32 m at $x=8$; $x^2-16x+48=0$: $x=4$, $12$, width 8 m"},{"q":"A rectangle with perimeter 50 m has area at least 150 m². For what $x$ is $P\\ge600$?","a":"$x^2-60x+800\\le0$: $20\\le x\\le40$"},{"q":"A motorbike starts from rest with $s=1.5t^2$ while a lorry 24 m ahead moves at 9 m/s. Find its greatest height and where it lands.","a":"5.5 m at $x=4$; lands at $x=4+\\sqrt{22}\\approx8.69$ m"}],"theory":[{"q":"(a) Copy and complete the table for $y=2x^2-x-10$ for $-3\\le x\\le3$. (b) Draw the graph. (c) From your graph find (i) the range of values of $x$ for which $y$ decreases as $x$ increases (ii) the range of values of $x$ for which $y<0$ (iii) the values of $x$ for which $y\\ge-4$. (d) Check (ii) and (iii) algebraically.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $x$: −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3; $y$: 11, 0, −7, −10, −9, −4, 5."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) A U-shaped curve with line of symmetry $x=\\tfrac14$ and minimum about $-10.1$."},{"k":"p","text":"(c)(i) $x<0.25$."},{"k":"p","text":"(ii) The roots are $-2$ and $2.5$, so $y<0$ for $-2<x<2.5$."},{"k":"p","text":"(iii) Draw $y=-4$: it meets the curve at $x=-1.5$ and $x=2$. $y\\ge-4$ for $x\\le-1.5$ or $x\\ge2$."},{"k":"p","text":"(d) (ii) $2x^2-x-10=(2x-5)(x+2)<0$: $-2<x<2.5$ ✓. (iii) $2x^2-x-6\\ge0$: $(2x+3)(x-2)\\ge0$: $x\\le-1.5$ or $x\\ge2$ ✓."}]},{"q":"A footballer kicks a ball from the ground. Its height after $t$ seconds is $h=19.6t-4.9t^2$ metres. (a) Tabulate $h$ for $t=0, 0.5, 1, \\dots, 4$ and draw the graph. (b) Find the maximum height and when it occurs. (c) For how long is the ball higher than 14.7 m? (d) A defender can head the ball only when it is between 1.5 m and 2.5 m high on its way down. Estimate this time interval from the graph.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $h$: 0, 8.575, 14.7, 18.375, 19.6, 18.375, 14.7, 8.575, 0."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) Vertex at $t=2$: $h=39.2-19.6=19.6$ m."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) $19.6t-4.9t^2=14.7$ gives $t^2-4t+3=0$, $t=1$ or $3$; so for $3-1=2$ seconds."},{"k":"p","text":"(d) On the way down, $h=2.5$: $4.9t^2-19.6t+2.5=0$, $t=\\dfrac{19.6+\\sqrt{384.16-49}}{9.8}\\approx3.87$. $h=1.5$: $4.9t^2-19.6t+1.5=0$, $t\\approx3.92$. So between about 3.87 s and 3.92 s: a window of only about 0.05 s, which is why heading a dropping ball needs good timing."}]},{"q":"A farmer has 120 m of fencing to enclose a rectangular pen divided into two equal parts by one extra fence parallel to the width. (a) If the width is $x$ m, show that the length is $(60-1.5x)$ m and the area is $A=60x-1.5x^2$. (b) Find the range of $x$ for which $A\\ge450$. (c) Find the largest possible area and the dimensions. (d) State the domain of $x$ and explain it.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Three widths and two lengths: $3x+2L=120$, so $L=60-1.5x$ and $A=x(60-1.5x)=60x-1.5x^2$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) $60x-1.5x^2\\ge450$ gives $1.5x^2-60x+450\\le0$, $x^2-40x+300\\le0$, $(x-10)(x-30)\\le0$: $10\\le x\\le30$."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) Vertex at $x=\\dfrac{60}{3}=20$: $A=1200-600=600$ m². Width 20 m, length 30 m."},{"k":"p","text":"(d) $0<x<40$: both the width and the length $60-1.5x$ must be positive."}]},{"q":"The cost of producing $x$ chairs a day is $C=x^2+10x+400$ (GH₵) and each chair sells for GH₵70. (a) Write the daily profit $P$ in terms of $x$. (b) For what daily outputs does the workshop make a profit? (c) For what outputs does the profit increase as $x$ increases? (d) Find the maximum profit. (e) Explain what happens to profit if the workshop makes more than the best number of chairs.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $P=70x-(x^2+10x+400)=-x^2+60x-400$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) $P>0$: $x^2-60x+400<0$; roots $x=30\\pm\\sqrt{500}\\approx7.6$ and $52.4$. For a triangle this is the **circumcircle**, and $O$ is the **circumcentre**."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w10-circum","caption":"Two perpendicular bisectors locate the centre."}],"figs":["w10-circum"]},{"title":"The circle theorems","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"We say a chord or arc **subtends** an angle at a point when the angle is formed by lines from its ends to that point."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Angle theorems","blocks":[{"k":"ol","items":["The angle subtended by an arc at the **centre** is **twice** the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining circumference.","The angle in a **semicircle** is a right angle.","Angles subtended by the same arc **in the same segment** are equal.","**Equal chords** subtend equal angles at the centre.","Conversely, if two chords subtend equal angles at the centre, the chords are equal.","Opposite angles of a **cyclic quadrilateral** add up to $180^\\circ$; so an **exterior** angle equals the **interior opposite** angle.","The angle between a **tangent** and a **chord** at the point of contact equals the angle in the **alternate segment**."]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w10-thm123","caption":"Theorems 1, 2 and 3."},{"k":"fig","id":"w10-thm67","caption":"Theorem 6 (cyclic quadrilateral) and theorem 7 (alternate segment)."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Chord properties","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["The perpendicular from the centre to a chord **bisects** the chord; conversely, the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it.","Equal chords are **equidistant** from the centre.","The radius drawn to a point of contact is **perpendicular** to the tangent (Week 11)."]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w10-chord","caption":"The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord."}],"figs":["w10-thm123","w10-thm67","w10-chord"]},{"title":"Proofs","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Proof of theorem 1","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Join $C$ to $O$ and extend to $D$ (Figure 10.6). $OA=OC=OB$ (radii), so triangles $AOC$ and $BOC$ are isosceles: $\\angle OAC=\\angle OCA=p$ and $\\angle OBC=\\angle OCB=s$. The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles, so $\\angle AOD=2p$ and $\\angle BOD=2s$. Hence $\\angle AOB=2p+2s=2(p+s)=2\\angle ACB$. $\\blacksquare$"}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w10-proof1","caption":"Two isosceles triangles prove theorem 1."},{"k":"ul","items":["**Theorem 2** follows from theorem 1: a diameter $AB$ subtends a straight angle, $180^\\circ$, at the centre, so the angle at the circumference is $\\tfrac12\\times180^\\circ=90^\\circ$.","**Theorem 3:** each angle in the same segment is half of the same angle at the centre, so they are equal.","**Theorem 4:** if $AB=XY$, triangles $AOB$ and $XOY$ have three pairs of equal sides (two radii and the equal chords), so they are congruent (SSS) and $\\angle AOB=\\angle XOY$.","**Theorem 5:** if $\\angle AOB=\\angle COD$, triangles $AOB$ and $COD$ are congruent (SAS: two radii and the included angle), so $AB=CD$.","**Theorem 6:** the two opposite angles stand on arcs that together make the whole circle, so the angles at the centre add to $360^\\circ$ and the angles at the circumference to $180^\\circ$."]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Give a reason for every step","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"In circle questions each angle must be justified: “angle at centre = twice angle at circumference”, “angles in the same segment”, “opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral”, “base angles of an isosceles triangle (radii)”, “angle in a semicircle”, “alternate segment theorem”. (c) Find the area of the original table top, to the nearest 100 cm².","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Draw any two non-parallel chords on the curved edge and construct their perpendicular bisectors. (b) Write about a page on how circle theorems are used in real life, with at least three examples.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) A good answer states each theorem precisely, draws a diagram marking the equal angles or right angle, and works one example with reasons. A circle has infinitely many tangents, one at each point."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Theorem: tangent ⟂ radius","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The tangent at any point of a circle is **perpendicular** to the radius drawn to the point of contact."},{"k":"p","text":"*Proof.* Let $L$ touch the circle at $A$, and let $B$ be any other point of $L$. $B$ lies outside the circle, so $OB$ crosses the circle at some point $C$, and $OB=OC+CB>OC=OA$. So $OA$ is the shortest distance from $O$ to $L$. The shortest segment from a point to a line is the perpendicular, so $OA\\perp L$. $\\blacksquare$"}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w11-perp","caption":"$OA$ is the shortest distance from $O$ to $L$."},{"k":"p","text":"Conversely, a line through a point of the circle that is perpendicular to the radius there is a tangent. To **construct the tangent at $A$**, draw the radius $OA$, extend it, and construct the perpendicular to $OA$ at $A$."}],"figs":["w11-perp"]},{"title":"Tangents from an external point","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Theorem: equal tangents","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The two tangents drawn to a circle from an external point $P$ are **equal** in length: $PA=PB$. Moreover, $OP$ **bisects** $\\angle APB$ and $\\angle AOB$, and $OP$ is the **perpendicular bisector** of the chord of contact $AB$."},{"k":"p","text":"*Proof.* In triangles $OAP$ and $OBP$: $\\angle OAP=\\angle OBP=90^\\circ$ (tangent ⟂ radius), $OP$ is a common hypotenuse and $OA=OB$ (radii). So the triangles are congruent (RHS), giving $PA=PB$, $\\angle APO=\\angle BPO$ and $\\angle AOP=\\angle BOP$. $\\blacksquare$"}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w11-equal","caption":"Two congruent right-angled triangles."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Useful results","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Tangent length from $P$: $PA^2=OP^2-r^2$.","In quadrilateral $OAPB$: $\\angle AOB+\\angle APB=180^\\circ$ (two right angles).","Triangle $PAB$ is isosceles, so $\\angle PAB=\\angle PBA=\\dfrac{180^\\circ-\\angle APB}{2}$."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"To **construct the tangents from $P$**: bisect $OP$ at $M$ and draw the circle with centre $M$ through $O$ and $P$. It cuts the given circle at $A$ and $B$, and $PA$, $PB$ are the tangents, because $\\angle OAP$ and $\\angle OBP$ are angles in a semicircle."},{"k":"fig","id":"w11-construct","caption":"The circle on $OP$ as diameter gives the points of contact."}],"figs":["w11-equal","w11-construct"]},{"title":"The alternate segment theorem","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Theorem: alternate segment","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The angle between a tangent and a chord drawn through the point of contact equals the angle subtended by the chord in the **alternate segment** (the segment on the other side of the chord)."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w11-altproof","caption":"Proof of the alternate segment theorem."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Proof","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Let $DAE$ be the tangent at $A$, $AB$ the chord, $\\angle BAE=x$, and $C$ a point in the alternate segment. $\\angle OAE=90^\\circ$, so $\\angle OAB=90^\\circ-x$. $OA=OB$, so $\\angle OBA=90^\\circ-x$ and $\\angle AOB=180^\\circ-2(90^\\circ-x)=2x$. By the angle-at-the-centre theorem, $\\angle ACB=\\tfrac12\\angle AOB=x$. $\\blacksquare$"}]},{"k":"p","text":"In a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ with tangent $DAE$ at $A$, the theorem combines with the opposite-angle theorem: each angle between the tangent and a side equals the angle at the far vertex across that side."}],"figs":["w11-altproof"]},{"title":"Inscribed circles and common tangents","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **inscribed circle** (incircle) of a triangle touches all three sides; its centre, the **incentre**, is where the angle bisectors meet. Since tangents from each vertex are equal, the tangent lengths are $s-a$, $s-b$ and $s-c$, where $s=\\tfrac12(a+b+c)$ is the semi-perimeter, and the radius is $r=\\dfrac{\\text{area}}{s}$."},{"k":"p","text":"A quadrilateral with an inscribed circle has $AB+CD=BC+DA$ (sums of opposite sides equal)."},{"k":"fig","id":"w11-incircle","caption":"Equal tangents from each vertex."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Common tangents of two circles","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For circles of radii $R$ and $r$ with centres $d$ apart:"},{"k":"ul","items":["direct (open belt) common tangent: $\\sqrt{d^2-(R-r)^2}$;","transverse (crossed belt) common tangent: $\\sqrt{d^2-(R+r)^2}$."]}]},{"k":"box","kind":"life","title":"Tangents in real life","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A bicycle chain and a car fan belt run along common tangents of two wheels; a road leaving a roundabout is built along a tangent so cars do not swerve; a satellite dish, a lighthouse beam or a sniper’s line of sight just grazing the Earth meets it along a tangent, which is how the distance to the horizon is calculated."}]}],"figs":["w11-incircle"]}],"examples":[{"title":"A tangent and an isosceles triangle","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$AC$ is a tangent to a circle with centre $O$ at $B$, and $D$ is a point on the circle, on the same side of $OB$ as $A$, with $\\angle BOD=120^\\circ$. (Check: $\\angle AOB=\\angle ACB=50^\\circ$, so $\\angle AOC=107^\\circ$ and $73^\\circ+107^\\circ=180^\\circ$ ✓.)","(ii) $\\angle AOE=\\angle ABO=40^\\circ$ (alternate segment). Then $x=21-14=7$, $y=21-15=6$, $z=21-13=8$.","(b) Heron: area $=\\sqrt{21\\times7\\times6\\times8}=\\sqrt{7056}=84$ cm².","The area is also $\\tfrac12r(a+b+c)=rs$, so $r=\\dfrac{84}{21}=4$ cm."],"answer":"(a) 7, 6 and 8 cm (b) 4 cm","figs":[]},{"title":"A circle inside a quadrilateral","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A circle is inscribed in quadrilateral $ABCD$, touching all four sides. $AB=9$ cm, $BC=11$ cm and $CD=8$ cm. (b) Hence prove that the line joining the external point to the centre bisects the angle between the tangents. (c) Prove that this line is perpendicular to the chord of contact.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Let $PA$, $PB$ touch the circle (centre $O$) at $A$ and $B$. In triangles $OAP$ and $OBP$: $\\angle OAP=\\angle OBP=90^\\circ$ (tangent ⟂ radius), $OP$ is common, and $OA=OB$ (radii). So the triangles are congruent (RHS) and $PA=PB$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) From the congruence, $\\angle APO=\\angle BPO$, so $PO$ bisects $\\angle APB$ (and $\\angle AOP=\\angle BOP$)."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) Let $OP$ meet $AB$ at $M$. In triangles $APM$ and $BPM$: $PA=PB$, $\\angle APM=\\angle BPM$ and $PM$ is common, so they are congruent (SAS). Hence $AM=BM$ and $\\angle AMP=\\angle BMP$; these angles are equal and add to $180^\\circ$, so each is $90^\\circ$. So $OP$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$."}]},{"q":"$TA$ and $TB$ are tangents to a circle with centre $O$, and $C$ is a point on the major arc $AB$. $\\angle ATB=2x$. (a) Express $\\angle AOB$, $\\angle ACB$ and $\\angle TAB$ in terms of $x$. (b) Show that $\\angle TAB=\\angle ACB$ and explain which theorem this illustrates. (c) If $x=25^\\circ$ and the radius is 8 cm, find $TA$.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $\\angle AOB=180^\\circ-2x$; $\\angle ACB=\\tfrac12(180^\\circ-2x)=90^\\circ-x$; $\\angle TAB=\\dfrac{180^\\circ-2x}{2}=90^\\circ-x$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) Both equal $90^\\circ-x$. $TA$ is a tangent and $AB$ a chord, and $C$ is in the alternate segment: this is the alternate segment theorem."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) $\\angle ATO=x=25^\\circ$, and in right triangle $OAT$: $\\tan25^\\circ=\\dfrac{8}{TA}$, so $TA=\\dfrac{8}{\\tan25^\\circ}\\approx17.16$ cm."}]},{"q":"(a) Prove the alternate segment theorem. (b) In the figure, $PQ$ is a tangent at $A$, $ABCD$ is cyclic, $\\angle PAD=50^\\circ$, $\\angle QAB=62^\\circ$ and $\\angle BDC=28^\\circ$. Find $\\angle ABD$, $\\angle ADB$, $\\angle BAD$, $\\angle BAC$ and $\\angle BCD$.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) As in the notes: with $\\angle BAE=x$, $\\angle OAB=90^\\circ-x$, $\\angle OBA=90^\\circ-x$, so $\\angle AOB=2x$, and the angle in the alternate segment is $\\tfrac12\\angle AOB=x$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) $\\angle ABD=\\angle PAD=50^\\circ$ (alternate segment, chord $AD$). $\\angle ADB=\\angle QAB=62^\\circ$ (alternate segment, chord $AB$). $\\angle BAD=180^\\circ-50^\\circ-62^\\circ=68^\\circ$. $\\angle BAC=\\angle BDC=28^\\circ$ (same segment, chord $BC$). $\\angle BCD=180^\\circ-68^\\circ=112^\\circ$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral)."}]},{"q":"A bicycle has a front chain wheel of radius 9 cm and a rear sprocket of radius 3 cm, with centres 40 cm apart. The chain runs round both along the two direct common tangents. (a) Find the length of each straight part of the chain. (b) Find the angle $\\theta$ that each radius to a point of contact makes with the line of centres. (c) Hence find the total length of the chain, to the nearest centimetre.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $\\sqrt{40^2-(9-3)^2}=\\sqrt{1564}\\approx39.55$ cm."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) $\\cos\\theta=\\dfrac{9-3}{40}=0.15$, so $\\theta\\approx81.37^\\circ$."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) On the large wheel the chain wraps the arc away from the small wheel: angle $360^\\circ-2\\theta\\approx197.25^\\circ$; on the small wheel it wraps $2\\theta\\approx162.75^\\circ$."},{"k":"p","text":"Arcs: $\\dfrac{197.25}{360}\\times2\\pi\\times9\\approx30.98$ cm and $\\dfrac{162.75}{360}\\times2\\pi\\times3\\approx8.52$ cm."},{"k":"p","text":"Total $\\approx2\\times39.55+30.98+8.52\\approx118.6$, about 119 cm."}]},{"q":"A right-angled triangle has legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$. (a) Show that the radius of its inscribed circle is $r=\\dfrac{a+b-c}{2}$ by using equal tangents. (b) Check the formula for the 3–4–5 triangle and the 5–12–13 triangle. (c) A triangular plot has sides 20 m, 21 m and 29 m. Find the radius of the largest circular fountain that fits inside it.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) At the right angle the two tangent lengths and two radii form a square of side $r$. So the tangent lengths from the acute vertices are $a-r$ and $b-r$, and these add up to the hypotenuse: $(a-r)+(b-r)=c$, giving $r=\\dfrac{a+b-c}{2}$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) $3$–$4$–$5$: $r=\\dfrac{3+4-5}{2}=1$. $5$–$12$–$13$: $r=\\dfrac{5+12-13}{2}=2$. Then $\\angle XOZ=120^\\circ+30^\\circ=150^\\circ$.","**Method 2.** Construct $OS\\perp$ the line at $O$, so $\\angle XOS=90^\\circ$. Bisect the right angle between it and the left-hand part of the line ($180^\\circ$): the bisector is at $90^\\circ+45^\\circ=135^\\circ$.","(b) First construct $150^\\circ$ (Example 12.1). Then bisect the $30^\\circ$ angle between the $150^\\circ$ ray and the left-hand part of the line: $150^\\circ+15^\\circ=165^\\circ$."],"answer":"(a) bisect between $90^\\circ$ and $180^\\circ$ (b) bisect between $150^\\circ$ and $180^\\circ$","figs":[]},{"title":"Halves of standard angles","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Plan the construction of (a) $22\\tfrac12^\\circ$ (b) $67\\tfrac12^\\circ$ (c) $37\\tfrac12^\\circ$ (d) $52\\tfrac12^\\circ$."}],"steps":["(a) Construct $90^\\circ$, bisect to get $45^\\circ$, bisect again: $22\\tfrac12^\\circ$.","(b) Construct $45^\\circ$ and $90^\\circ$ on the same side; bisect between them: $45^\\circ+22\\tfrac12^\\circ=67\\tfrac12^\\circ$.","(c) Construct $75^\\circ$ and bisect it: $37\\tfrac12^\\circ$.","(d) Construct $105^\\circ$ and bisect it: $52\\tfrac12^\\circ$."],"answer":"(a) $\\tfrac14$ of $90^\\circ$ (b) between $45^\\circ$ and $90^\\circ$ (c) $\\tfrac12$ of $75^\\circ$ (d) $\\tfrac12$ of $105^\\circ$","figs":[]},{"title":"Can it be constructed?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Which of these angles can be constructed exactly with ruler and compasses using the methods above? construct the angles at its ends (find the third angle first if needed)"],["RHS: right angle, hypotenuse, side","construct the right angle; mark the side; arc of the hypotenuse length"]]},{"k":"p","text":"For SSS the sum of any two sides must exceed the third (the **triangle inequality**), or the arcs do not meet."},{"k":"fig","id":"w13-sss","caption":"Two arcs fix the third vertex."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"The ambiguous case (SSA)","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"If two sides and a **non-included** angle are given (for example $AB$, $AC$ and $\\angle B$), the arc for $AC$ may cut the other arm of $\\angle B$ at **two** points. This happens when $AB\\sin B<AC<AB$."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w13-ambig","caption":"Two triangles from the same SSA data."}],"figs":["w13-sss","w13-ambig"]},{"title":"Constructing quadrilaterals","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A quadrilateral needs **five** independent pieces of data (for example three sides and two angles). There may be two, one or no such points; always check the question’s other conditions (inside the shape, nearer one town, and so on)."},{"k":"p","text":"Inequalities give **regions**: “less than 4 cm from $A$” is the inside of a circle; “nearer to $B$ than to $C$” is the side of the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ that contains $B$. With centre $A$ and radius 8 cm draw an arc; with centre $C$ and radius 9 cm draw an arc to cut it at $B$. Join $AB$ and $CB$.","(b) $\\angle BAC$ should measure about $59^\\circ$.","(c) Cosine rule: $\\cos A=\\dfrac{8^2+10^2-9^2}{2(8)(10)}=\\dfrac{83}{160}$, so $\\angle A\\approx58.75^\\circ$."],"answer":"$\\angle BAC\\approx58.75^\\circ$","figs":[]},{"title":"Two sides and the included angle","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Construct triangle $XYZ$ with $XY=12$ cm, $XZ=10$ cm and $\\angle YXZ=75^\\circ$. Measure $YZ$ and check it by calculation."}],"steps":["Draw $XY=12$ cm. At $X$ construct $75^\\circ$ (bisect between $60^\\circ$ and $90^\\circ$).","Mark $Z$ on the arm with $XZ=10$ cm; join $YZ$.","$YZ$ measures about 13.5 cm.","Check: $YZ^2=144+100-240\\cos75^\\circ=244-62.12=181.88$, $YZ\\approx13.49$ cm ✓."],"answer":"$YZ\\approx13.5$ cm","figs":[]},{"title":"One side and two angles","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Construct triangle $PQR$ with $QR=8$ cm, $\\angle PQR=105^\\circ$ and $\\angle PRQ=45^\\circ$. Measure and calculate (a) $PQ$ (b) $PR$."}],"steps":["Draw $QR=8$ cm. Construct $105^\\circ$ at $Q$ and $45^\\circ$ at $R$; the arms meet at $P$.","$\\angle QPR=180^\\circ-105^\\circ-45^\\circ=30^\\circ$.","(a) $PQ=\\dfrac{8\\sin45^\\circ}{\\sin30^\\circ}\\approx11.31$ cm.","(b) $PR=\\dfrac{8\\sin105^\\circ}{\\sin30^\\circ}\\approx15.45$ cm."],"answer":"(a) about 11.3 cm (b) about 15.5 cm","figs":[]},{"title":"The ambiguous case","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$AB=8$ cm, $AC=6$ cm and $\\angle ABC=40^\\circ$. (a) Show by construction that two triangles are possible. (b) Find both possible values of $\\angle ACB$ and of $BC$."}],"steps":["(a) Draw $\\angle ABC=40^\\circ$ with $BA=8$ cm on one arm. The arc of radius 6 cm centred at $A$ cuts the other arm at two points $C_1$ and $C_2$, because $8\\sin40^\\circ\\approx5.14<6<8$.","(b) Sine rule: $\\sin C=\\dfrac{8\\sin40^\\circ}{6}\\approx0.857$, so $C\\approx59.0^\\circ$ or $121.0^\\circ$.","If $C=59.0^\\circ$: $A=81.0^\\circ$, $BC=\\dfrac{6\\sin81^\\circ}{\\sin40^\\circ}\\approx9.22$ cm.","If $C=121.0^\\circ$: $A=19.0^\\circ$, $BC=\\dfrac{6\\sin19^\\circ}{\\sin40^\\circ}\\approx3.04$ cm."],"answer":"$\\angle C\\approx59^\\circ$ with $BC\\approx9.22$ cm, or $\\angle C\\approx121^\\circ$ with $BC\\approx3.04$ cm","figs":[]},{"title":"A trapezium","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Construct quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $AB=BC=11$ cm, $AD=7.5$ cm, $\\angle ABC=105^\\circ$ and $AD\\parallel BC$. (a) Explain how to construct the angle at $A$. (b) Measure $DC$. (c) Calculate $DC$ and the area."}],"steps":["Draw $AB=11$ cm and construct $105^\\circ$ at $B$; mark $C$ with $BC=11$ cm.","(a) $AD\\parallel BC$, so the co-interior angles at $A$ and $B$ add up to $180^\\circ$: $\\angle BAD=75^\\circ$. Construct $75^\\circ$ at $A$ and mark $D$ at 7.5 cm. Join $DC$.","(b) $DC$ measures about 12.4 cm.","(c) With $A=(0,0)$, $B=(11,0)$: $C=(11+11\\cos75^\\circ,\\,11\\sin75^\\circ)=(13.85,\\,10.63)$ and $D=(7.5\\cos75^\\circ,\\,7.5\\sin75^\\circ)=(1.94,\\,7.24)$. $DC=\\sqrt{11.91^2+3.38^2}\\approx12.38$ cm.","The distance between the parallel sides is $11\\sin75^\\circ\\approx10.63$ cm, so the area is $\\tfrac12(11+7.5)\\times10.63\\approx98.3$ cm²."],"answer":"(b), (c) $DC\\approx12.4$ cm; area about 98.3 cm²","figs":["w13-trap"]},{"title":"A rhombus from a side and a diagonal","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Construct a rhombus $PQRS$ with sides 6 cm and diagonal $PR=10$ cm. (a) Describe the construction. (b) Calculate the other diagonal and the angles."}],"steps":["(a) Draw $PR=10$ cm. With centres $P$ and $R$ and radius 6 cm, draw arcs on both sides of $PR$; they meet at $Q$ and $S$. Join $PQRS$.","(b) The diagonals bisect each other at right angles: half of $QS$ is $\\sqrt{6^2-5^2}=\\sqrt{11}$, so $QS=2\\sqrt{11}\\approx6.63$ cm.","$\\angle QPS=2\\cos^{-1}\\tfrac56\\approx2\\times33.56^\\circ=67.1^\\circ$, and $\\angle PQR=180^\\circ-67.1^\\circ=112.9^\\circ$."],"answer":"$QS\\approx6.63$ cm; angles $67.1^\\circ$ and $112.9^\\circ$","figs":[]},{"title":"Describing loci","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Describe the locus in each case. (a) A goat is tied to a peg by a 4 m rope: the boundary it can reach. (b) Points on a football field equidistant from the two goalposts of one goal. (c) Points equidistant from the walls $AB$ and $AD$ of a room. (d) Points 2 m from a straight fence. (e) A point equidistant from three villages."}],"steps":["(a) A circle of radius 4 m centred at the peg (the goat can graze the whole disc inside it).","(b) The perpendicular bisector of the line joining the goalposts.","(c) The bisector of the corner angle $DAB$.","(d) Two lines parallel to the fence, 2 m on each side (with semicircular ends at the ends of the fence).","(e) The circumcentre of the triangle formed by the villages."],"answer":"(a) circle (b) perpendicular bisector (c) angle bisector (d) two parallel lines (e) circumcentre","figs":[]},{"title":"The locus between two parallel lines","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$m_1$ and $m_2$ are parallel lines. Construct the locus $d$ of points equidistant from $m_1$ and $m_2$, and explain why it works."}],"steps":["At any point $O$ on $m_1$ construct the perpendicular, meeting $m_2$ at $A$.","Construct the perpendicular bisector of $OA$; call it $d$.","$d$ is perpendicular to $OA$, which is perpendicular to both lines, so $d$ is parallel to $m_1$ and $m_2$.","Every point of $d$ is at distance $\\tfrac12 OA$ from each line, so $d$ is the required locus."],"answer":"The perpendicular bisector of a common perpendicular $OA$.","figs":[]},{"title":"A parallelogram with two loci","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Construct parallelogram $PQRS$ with $PQ=8$ cm, $QR=6$ cm and diagonal $PR=11.5$ cm. (b) Construct the locus $u$ of points 5 cm from $Q$. (c) Construct the locus $t$ of points equidistant from $PS$ and $SR$. (d) Label the intersections of $u$ and $t$ as $A$ and $B$ and measure $AB$."}],"steps":["(a) Construct triangle $PQR$ by SSS. With centre $R$ and radius 8 cm, and centre $P$ and radius 6 cm, draw arcs meeting at $S$. Join $PS$ and $RS$.","(b) $u$ is the circle with centre $Q$ and radius 5 cm.","(c) $t$ is the bisector of $\\angle PSR$.","(d) $t$ cuts $u$ at $A$ (inside the parallelogram) and at $B$ (below $PQ$).","Calculation with $P=(0,0)$, $Q=(8,0)$: $R\\approx(10.02,\\,5.65)$, $S\\approx(2.02,\\,5.65)$; the bisector meets the circle at $A\\approx(3.94,\\,2.92)$ and $B\\approx(9.39,\\,-4.81)$, so $AB\\approx9.5$ cm."],"answer":"$AB\\approx9.5$ cm","figs":["w13-parallelogram"]},{"title":"A restaurant plan","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The floor of a restaurant is a quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $AB=6$ m, $BC=7.5$ m, $AD=5$ m, $\\angle DAB=105^\\circ$ and $\\angle ABC=90^\\circ$. (a) Using a scale of 1 cm to 1 m, construct the plan. (b) A washing basin $O$ is equidistant from $BC$ and $CD$ and exactly 5.5 m from $A$. Locate it. (c) Find the perimeter of the floor."}],"steps":["(a) Draw $AB=6$ cm; construct $90^\\circ$ at $B$ and mark $C$ with $BC=7.5$ cm; construct $105^\\circ$ at $A$ and mark $D$ with $AD=5$ cm; join $CD$.","(b) Points equidistant from $BC$ and $CD$ lie on the bisector of $\\angle BCD$. Points 5.5 m from $A$ lie on the circle with centre $A$ and radius 5.5 cm. $O$ is their intersection inside the room.","(c) $CD$ measures about 7.8 cm. Check: with $A=(0,0)$, $C=(6,\\,7.5)$ and $D=(5\\cos105^\\circ,\\,5\\sin105^\\circ)=(-1.29,\\,4.83)$: $CD=\\sqrt{7.29^2+2.67^2}\\approx7.77$ m.","Perimeter $\\approx6+7.5+7.77+5=26.3$ m.","By calculation, $O\\approx(3.64,\\,4.12)$: about 2.4 m from both $BC$ and $CD$."],"answer":"(c) about 26.3 m; $O$ is about 2.4 m from walls $BC$ and $CD$","figs":["w13-restaurant"]},{"title":"Siting a market","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Town $M$ is 20 km from $N$ and 22 km from $P$, and $N$ is 18 km from $P$. A market must be equidistant from $N$ and $M$ and exactly 10 km from $P$. (a) Using a scale of 1 cm to 2 km, find by construction the possible sites $A$ and $B$. (b) Find the distance between the sites. (c) Find their distances from $N$. (d) Which site is more convenient? Justify."}],"steps":["(a) Construct triangle $MNP$ by SSS ($NM=10$ cm, $NP=9$ cm, $MP=11$ cm). Construct the perpendicular bisector of $NM$ and the circle with centre $P$ and radius 5 cm. They meet at $A$ and $B$.","Calculation: with $N=(0,0)$ and $M=(20,0)$, $P=(6,\\,16.97)$. The bisector is $x=10$; $(10-6)^2+(y-16.97)^2=100$ gives $y=16.97\\pm9.17$.","(b) $AB=2\\times9.17\\approx18.3$ km.","(c) $A=(10,\\,7.81)$: $AN=\\sqrt{100+60.9}\\approx12.7$ km. $B=(10,\\,26.14)$: $BN\\approx28.0$ km.","(d) Site $A$: it is 12.7 km from both $N$ and $M$ (instead of 28.0 km) and still 10 km from $P$, so total travel is much less."],"answer":"(b) about 18.3 km (c) $AN\\approx12.7$ km, $BN\\approx28.0$ km (d) $A$","figs":["w13-market"]},{"title":"A region of points","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$ABC$ is an equilateral triangle of side 8 cm. Find the area of $R$."}],"steps":["Construct the triangle (all arcs of radius 8 cm).","“Less than 4 cm from $A$”: inside the circle with centre $A$, radius 4 cm.","“Nearer to $B$ than to $C$”: on $B$’s side of the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, which passes through $A$ (the triangle is equilateral).","$R$ is the sector of the circle between $AB$ and the bisector: angle $30^\\circ$ at $A$.","Area $=\\dfrac{30}{360}\\times\\pi\\times4^2=\\dfrac{4\\pi}{3}\\approx4.19$ cm²."],"answer":"A $30^\\circ$ sector of radius 4 cm; area about 4.19 cm²","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results","items":["Triangles: SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS, RHS; SSA may give two triangles when $AB\\sin B<AC<AB$.","Quadrilaterals need five pieces of data; use parallel-line and diagonal properties.","Loci: circle (one point), perpendicular bisector (two points), angle bisector (two lines), midline (two parallel lines), parallel pair (one line), circumcentre (three points).","Points satisfying two conditions lie at intersections of loci; inequalities give regions.","Check scale drawings with the sine and cosine rules or coordinates."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"Which set of lengths cannot form a triangle?","options":["3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm","5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm","4 cm, 4 cm, 7 cm","6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm"],"correct":0,"explain":"$3+4<8$."},{"q":"The locus of points equidistant from two points $A$ and $B$ is","options":["the perpendicular bisector of $AB$","the circle with diameter $AB$","the line $AB$","the bisector of an angle at $A$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Every point on it is the same distance from $A$ and $B$."},{"q":"The locus of points 3 cm from a fixed point $P$ is","options":["a circle of radius 3 cm centred at $P$","a line 3 cm from $P$","a square of side 3 cm","two parallel lines"],"correct":0,"explain":"Constant distance from one point."},{"q":"The locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines is","options":["the bisectors of the angles between them","a circle","a line parallel to both","the perpendicular bisector of one line"],"correct":0,"explain":"Angle bisectors."},{"q":"In a trapezium $ABCD$ with $AD\\parallel BC$ and $\\angle ABC=110^\\circ$, $\\angle BAD=$","options":["$70^\\circ$","$110^\\circ$","$90^\\circ$","$55^\\circ$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Co-interior angles sum to $180^\\circ$."},{"q":"The point equidistant from three villages is found by intersecting","options":["two perpendicular bisectors","two angle bisectors","two medians","two altitudes"],"correct":0,"explain":"It is the circumcentre."},{"q":"Given $AB=10$, $\\angle B=30^\\circ$ and $AC=7$, the number of possible triangles is","options":["2","1","0","3"],"correct":0,"explain":"$10\\sin30^\\circ=5<7<10$."},{"q":"A rhombus has side 5 cm and one diagonal 8 cm. The other diagonal is","options":["6 cm","3 cm","4 cm","9.4 cm"],"correct":0,"explain":"$2\\sqrt{25-16}$."},{"q":"The region “nearer to $B$ than to $C$” is bounded by","options":["the perpendicular bisector of $BC$","the circle on $BC$ as diameter","the line $BC$","the bisector of angle $B$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Points on the bisector are equally near both."},{"q":"A goat tied to the middle of a 6 m straight rail by a 2 m rope can reach a region bounded by","options":["two parallel segments and two semicircles","a circle of radius 2 m","a circle of radius 8 m","a rectangle 6 m by 2 m"],"correct":0,"explain":"Points within 2 m of a segment."}],"exercise":[{"q":"Construct triangle $LMN$ with $LM=7$ cm, $MN=8$ cm and $LN=9$ cm. Calculate $BC$.","a":"$BC^2=81+36-54=63$: $BC\\approx7.94$ cm"},{"q":"Construct triangle $PQR$ with $PQ=10$ cm, $\\angle P=45^\\circ$, $\\angle Q=75^\\circ$. Calculate $QR$.","a":"$\\angle R=60^\\circ$: $QR=\\tfrac{10\\sin45^\\circ}{\\sin60^\\circ}\\approx8.16$ cm"},{"q":"For $AB=9$ cm, $AC=7$ cm and $\\angle B=35^\\circ$, show that two triangles are possible and find both values of $\\angle C$.","a":"$9\\sin35^\\circ\\approx5.16<7<9$; $\\sin C\\approx0.737$: $47.5^\\circ$ or $132.5^\\circ$"},{"q":"Construct parallelogram $ABCD$ with $AB=7$ cm, $AD=5$ cm and $\\angle DAB=60^\\circ$. Calculate both diagonals.","a":"$BD=\\sqrt{39}\\approx6.24$ cm, $AC=\\sqrt{109}\\approx10.44$ cm"},{"q":"Construct a rhombus with diagonals 8 cm and 6 cm. Find its side and angles.","a":"5 cm; $2\\tan^{-1}\\tfrac34\\approx73.7^\\circ$ and $106.3^\\circ$"},{"q":"Construct trapezium $PQRS$ with $PQ\\parallel SR$, $PQ=9$ cm, $\\angle P=60^\\circ$, $PS=5$ cm and $SR=5$ cm. Calculate $QR$.","a":"$S=(2.5,\\,4.33)$, $R=(7.5,\\,4.33)$: $QR=\\sqrt{1.5^2+4.33^2}\\approx4.58$ cm"},{"q":"Two trees are 30 m apart. Describe the locus of points equidistant from them and the locus of points 20 m from the first tree, and find the distance between the two points that satisfy both.","a":"Perpendicular bisector and circle: $2\\sqrt{20^2-15^2}\\approx26.5$ m"},{"q":"In triangle $ABC$ with $AB=8$, $BC=7$, $CA=6$ cm, construct the point equidistant from $A$, $B$ and $C$, and calculate the radius of the circle through them.","a":"$R=\\dfrac{a}{2\\sin A}$; $\\cos A=\\tfrac{64+36-49}{96}$, $A\\approx57.9^\\circ$: $R\\approx4.13$ cm"},{"q":"A security light at a corner of a 20 m by 12 m yard lights everything within 15 m. What fraction of the yard is lit? Describe the region.","a":"A triangle (area 54 m²) plus a $53.1^\\circ$ sector of radius 15 m (area 104.3 m²): 158.3 m², about 66% of the yard"},{"q":"Construct the region inside a square of side 6 cm that is nearer to side $AB$ than to side $AD$ and more than 3 cm from $C$.","a":"Region on $AB$’s side of the diagonal $AC$, outside the circle of radius 3 about $C$; area $18-\\tfrac{9\\pi}{8}\\approx14.47$ cm²"},{"q":"Points $A$ and $B$ are 10 cm apart. Find the area of the region of points less than 6 cm from both $A$ and $B$.","a":"Lens of two circles: $2(36\\cos^{-1}\\tfrac56-5\\sqrt{11})\\approx9.0$ cm²"}],"theory":[{"q":"(a) Using ruler and compasses only, construct triangle $ABC$ with $AB=10$ cm, $\\angle ABC=60^\\circ$ and $BC=7$ cm. (b) Construct the locus of points equidistant from $A$ and $C$, and the locus of points equidistant from $AB$ and $BC$. (c) Label their intersection $X$ and measure $BX$. (d) Calculate $AC$ and $BX$.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Draw $AB=10$ cm, construct $60^\\circ$ at $B$ and mark $C$ at 7 cm."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) The perpendicular bisector of $AC$, and the bisector of $\\angle ABC$."},{"k":"p","text":"(c), (d) $AC^2=100+49-70=79$, so $AC\\approx8.89$ cm. Take $B=(0,0)$, $A=(10,0)$ and $C=(3.5,\\,6.06)$. The angle bisector at $B$ makes $30^\\circ$ with $BA$, so $X=(0.866t,\\,0.5t)$ where $t=BX$. Setting $XA^2=XC^2$: $t^2-17.32t+100=t^2-12.12t+49$, so $5.20t=51$ and $t\\approx9.81$. Hence $BX\\approx9.8$ cm, which the measurement should match."}]},{"q":"A village water committee wants a borehole that is equidistant from the school $S$ and the clinic $C$, which are 600 m apart, and within 400 m of the chief’s palace $P$, which is 500 m from $S$ and 700 m from $C$. (a) Using a scale of 1 cm to 100 m, construct triangle $SCP$. (b) Construct the locus of points equidistant from $S$ and $C$ and the region within 400 m of $P$. (c) Describe where the borehole may be placed, and find the nearest such point to $S$.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Draw $SC=6$ cm and arcs of 5 cm from $S$ and 7 cm from $C$ to locate $P$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) The perpendicular bisector of $SC$ and the disc of radius 4 cm centred at $P$."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) The borehole may be anywhere on the part of the perpendicular bisector inside the circle. With $S=(0,0)$, $C=(6,0)$: $P=(1,\\,4.90)$ (since $x^2+y^2=25$, $(x-6)^2+y^2=49$ gives $x=1$). The bisector $x=3$ meets the circle where $(y-4.90)^2=16-4=12$, $y=4.90\\pm3.46$: from $(3,\\,1.44)$ to $(3,\\,8.36)$. The nearest point to $S$ is $(3,\\,1.44)$: about $\\sqrt{9+2.07}\\approx3.33$ cm, that is 333 m from $S$ (and from $C$)."}]},{"q":"(a) Explain why the angle-bisector construction gives the locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines. (b) Explain why the bisectors of the four angles formed by two crossing lines form two perpendicular lines. (c) Hence describe the locus of points equidistant from three lines that form a triangle, inside the triangle.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Let $X$ be on the bisector of $\\angle AOB$. Drop perpendiculars $XM$ and $XN$ to the arms. Triangles $OMX$ and $ONX$ have $\\angle M=\\angle N=90^\\circ$, $\\angle MOX=\\angle NOX$ and $OX$ common, so they are congruent (AAS) and $XM=XN$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) Adjacent angles at the crossing add up to $180^\\circ$; their bisectors make $\\tfrac12$ of each, so the angle between the bisectors is $\\tfrac12\\times180^\\circ=90^\\circ$."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) A point equidistant from all three sides lies on the bisectors of all three angles.
